rv.q: But this engrossing production mostly gets the measure of the trilogy.
The two-hour stage piece often falters only to be saved by blessed moments of sheer brilliance.

Technically, it’s striking and impressive but a fine production can’t quite compensate for the fact that, in turning three books into a fairly short play with only six actors, Reader’s adaptation sometimes feels like a symphony rescored for a sextet who can’t quite hit the right notes.
The stylised writing leans heavily on subtext producing dialogue that at times appears stilted.

However, its considerable potential is not fully realised, with the emotional distance from its characters ultimately limiting the power of its exploration of loneliness, exploitation and human connection.
It’s sublimely realised in sleaze too by the predominantly youthful company led by the magisterial Maloney, fresh out of his latest Poirrot.
It is a play which handles the emptiness of these characters, and their desperation to fill it, with some success, although ironically also finding that same sense of hollowness in itself.
The cast play it out brilliantly, but ultimately the script is flat with no life-shaking reversals, just a simple representation of unrequited love in unsuitable relationships which would never work.

cn.t: Hamilton's bleak 1920s London trilogy receives a mixed reception in this ambitious stage adaptation, with critics praising its atmospheric period detail but questioning whether three novels can effectively condense into two hours.
